1:
The chapter opens on a funeral and a succession, and the witnesses read the single verse as the deliberate seam by which the chronicler binds a good reign to the wicked one that follows. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott keeps close to the wording: "Now" is simply "And," "slept" is "lay down," and the whole sentence, he observes, stands literally the same as the notice of Jehoshaphat's death already given at 1 Kings 22:50. The reformed John Gill glosses the idiom in his usual brief way — Jehoshaphat "slept with his fathers," that is, died as they died — and passes the reader on to the fuller record.

His fellow grammatical-historical witness Keil and Delitzsch explains why the death and burial of Jehoshaphat are carried over to open this chapter rather than to close the last: Joram's first act after his father's death stands in essential connection with that event, since he began his reign by murdering all his brothers, the sons of Jehoshaphat. They map the whole reign in advance — the body of the account, from v.5 onward, agrees almost word for word with the parallel at 2 Kings 8:17-22, but the chronicler inserts what Kings does not have: the letter of Elijah and the catalogue of divine chastisements inflicted on Joram for his crime, at vv.12-19.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry and the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke set the moral frame the bare verse implies. Henry sees the chapter as the tragedy of a house: a careful, indulgent father who secured the crown to a firstborn far less worthy than the brothers he portioned off, and a son who repaid that kindness with fratricide — "it is no new thing," Henry warns, "for the children that have been most indulged by their parents to be least dutiful to them." Clarke lays out the arc of the reign in a breath: Jehoram succeeds his father and commences his reign with the murder of his brethren and of several princes, walks in the way of Ahab whose daughter Athaliah he had married, provokes the revolt of Edom, is warned by a writing from Elijah, is plundered by Philistines and Arabians, and dies miserably of an incurable disease after a profligate reign of eight years.

The witnesses do not divide. Ellicott and Gill secure the text and its idiom; Keil explains the chronicler's stitching and flags the material he alone preserves; Henry and Clarke sound the note the whole chapter will carry — that a throne resting, for the covenant's sake, upon the house of David is about to be filled by a man who will do everything in his power to forfeit it.
2:
The chronicler names Jehoram's six brothers and calls their father "king of Israel," and it is that last phrase, not the roll of names, that divides the witnesses. The reformed John Gill notes simply that these were the sons of Jehoshaphat whom Jehoram succeeded. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch list them — Azariah, Jehiel, Zechariah, Azariah, Michael, and Shephatiah — and read the verse as the setup for the atrocity to come: these are the brethren Joram will presently slaughter, together with some of the princes of Israel, the tribal heads of his kingdom. They doubt the motive was mere avarice, a grasping after their property; more likely, they judge, the brothers were killed because they did not sympathize with the idolatrous course Joram and Athaliah were entering upon.

Over the title "king of Israel" the wesleyan-arminian witnesses take opposite roads. Adam Clarke declares it a plain corruption: Jehoshaphat was king of Judah, not of Israel, and the Hebrew "Yisrael" must here be an error for "Yehudah" — the very reading, he points out, of the Syriac, Arabic, Septuagint, and Vulgate, supported by thirty-eight of Kennicott's and De Rossi's manuscripts, so that "Judah" should be restored to the text. John Wesley, by contrast, lets the received word stand and finds a reason for it: Jehoshaphat is called king of Israel either because he was so by right, or because he reigned not over Judah and Benjamin only but over a great number of Israelites who had come and settled in his kingdom — the faithful refugees of the earlier chapters. So the debate is real: is "Israel" a scribe's slip to be corrected against the versions, or a meaningful title reflecting the godly northerners gathered under a righteous southern king?

Wesley adds a second small observation, that two of the brothers bear the same name, Azariah, doubtless distinguished in their own day by some further title which Scripture did not trouble to preserve, since it "did not concern succeeding ages to know it."

The witnesses do not, in the end, quarrel over the substance of the verse — six royal brothers, richly endowed, marked out by their very worth for destruction. Gill fixes them as Jehoshaphat's sons; Keil names them and reads their doom in their piety; Clarke and Wesley differ only over the one geographical word, whether to mend it or to make sense of it. Between them they set the stage for the fratricide that the next verses will unfold, and quietly underline how a house so carefully provided for could be so swiftly turned to blood.
3:
"Their father gave them great gifts... with fenced cities in Judah: but the kingdom gave he to Jehoram, because he was the firstborn." The witnesses weigh both the generosity of the father and the wisdom of his choice. The reformed John Gill likens the endowment to the patriarch's: Jehoshaphat dealt with his younger sons as Abraham did with the sons of his concubines, whom he sent away from Isaac "with gifts" rather than leaving them to contest the inheritance. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch note the substance of the settlement — silver, gold, and precious things, together with strong cities scattered through Judah — while the crown itself went undivided to Jehoram by the ancient right of the firstborn.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry admires the father's fairness and yet questions his policy. Jehoshaphat was a careful, indulgent father: he had many sons, and Scripture will say plainly at v.13 that they were better than Jehoram, of more wisdom and virtue, any of them fitter for the crown than he; yet because Jehoram was the eldest his father secured the kingdom to him and portioned the rest so that they should be easy and give him no disturbance. Herein, Henry allows, Jehoshaphat was kind and fair, and might have obliged a better son to tread in his steps. But whether he did well by his people Henry will not say; for Jehoram's birthright entitled him only to a double portion of the estate under the law of Deut. 21:17, and if he was manifestly unfit to govern it might have been better to set him aside for a worthier brother. Power is a sacred thing, Henry reasons, with which men may do much good or much hurt; and so he presses the old maxims, that he who deserves it should have it, and that the security of the people is the supreme law.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke turns from the gifts to the chronology hidden in the word "kingdom." Jehoshaphat, he explains, made Jehoram co-partner with himself in the throne about three years before his own death, so that Jehoram reigned only some five years after his father died — a reckoning Clarke ties to his fuller attempts to settle this disturbed chronology at 2 Kings 8:16 and 2 Chronicles 1:17.

The witnesses converge on a father's tragedy. Gill and Keil fix the endowment; Henry weighs the justice of preferring the firstborn; Clarke measures the years of the reign it opened. All see a good king providing generously for sons more deserving than the one to whom, by strict custom, he handed the kingdom — a provision that would shortly be repaid with their murder.
4:
When Jehoram had risen to his father's throne and made himself secure, he slew all his brethren with the sword, and certain of the princes of Israel besides — and the witnesses probe both the deed and the dark strength that steeled him to it. The reformed John Gill notes that he now "reigned alone," having shared the throne with his father for some years before. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch mark the verb "he strengthened himself," the same word used of Solomon's establishing at 2 Chronicles 1:1, and judge that Joram killed his brothers not from greed for their estates but because they would not sympathize with his political course and disapproved of the idolatry he and Athaliah were bringing in.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses sharpen both phrases. John Wesley reads "strengthened himself" as "hardened his heart," the sense the word sometimes carries, and identifies the murdered princes as the chief of those Israelites who out of love to God and true religion had forsaken their estates in the northern kingdom and joined themselves to Judah — men Jehoram struck down precisely because he knew they would be most zealous for the faith he was resolved to oppose. Adam Clarke turns the verse into a meditation on ambition: "what a truly diabolic thing is the lust of power!" — it destroys all the charities of life, so that this execrable man, to sit the more secure upon his throne, imbrued his hands in the blood of his own brothers; and Clarke observes that history furnishes more instances of such fratricide among bad Asiatic kings than among any other class of men.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the moral. Jehoram was a most barbarous brother, who as soon as he was settled slew all his brethren, whether by false accusation under colour of law or by plain assassination; and Henry reads his motive as Cain's — he hated and slew them because their piety condemned his impiety and had won them the esteem with the people that he had lost. "Those that mean ill themselves," Henry writes, "are commonly, without cause, jealous of those about them," and the wicked fear where no fear is. With the brethren he slew the princes who adhered to them, the true Israelites of integrity; and over the whole bloody foundation Henry pronounces the prophet's woe against him that foundeth a kingdom in blood, at Hab. 2:12 — a foundation that will sink the building raised upon it.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Keil fix the fact and the word; Wesley and Clarke expose the motive and the horror; Henry names the sin by its oldest name. All agree that a reign begun in fratricide has doomed itself before it has well started.
5:
"Jehoram was thirty and two years old when he began to reign, and he reigned eight years in Jerusalem." The witnesses pause over the accession-formula and the point at which the chronicler rejoins his older source. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch mark this verse as the head of the record of the duration and spirit of Joram's reign, and observe that from here onward the account runs parallel to 2 Kings 8:17-22, differing only in trifles that they had already weighed in commenting on that passage. The reformed John Gill likewise treats the verse as matter already handled and refers the reader back to the parallel record.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott adds the small grammatical touch that betrays the compiler's hand. Where the chronicler writes "Jehoram was thirty and two years old," the older text at 2 Kings 8:17 has merely "he was" — because there the king's name had just occurred in the previous verse, whereas the chronicler, taking up the notice afresh, must name him again. It is the kind of minute divergence by which the grammatical-historical eye follows one writer transcribing and lightly reshaping another.

The figures themselves the witnesses let carry their own weight. Thirty-two is the age not of a boy misled by evil counsellors but of a grown and responsible man; Jehoram sinned with his eyes open, in the full maturity of his powers, and the brevity of his reign — a bare eight years — is itself a silent verdict on a life that God would not suffer to run long. Keil and Delitzsch note further that the chronicler, having reached this point, will follow the framework of Kings for the political history — the accession, the apostasy, the covenant reservation, the revolt of Edom and of Libnah — before turning aside, from v.12, to the material he alone preserves: the letter of Elijah and the long catalogue of judgments upon this king's body, house, and memory.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill defers to the parallel; Keil fixes the verse as the seam where the two histories meet and lays out the course the chapter will take; Ellicott secures the grammar of the seam. Between them they show the chronicler at his work — a faithful editor who takes over the older annals almost word for word where they serve his purpose, and supplements them where he has a lesson to press that the older record did not stop to teach. The dry regnal notice is thus the threshold of the whole tragic reign, marking a man old enough to know better set for a short and evil eight years upon the throne of David.
11:
"Moreover he made high places in the mountains of Judah, and caused the inhabitants of Jerusalem to commit fornication, and compelled Judah thereto." The witnesses hear in the very grammar the measure of the king's guilt. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott marks the stress on the pronoun — he made — set in pointed contrast with Asa and Jehoshaphat, his worthier predecessors who had pulled such shrines down, as at 2 Chronicles 17:6; from this point, Ellicott notes, the narrative becomes peculiar to the chronicler, no longer shadowing the book of Kings. The high places he takes to be for the worship of foreign gods as well as of the God of Israel; and he records the textual ripple over "mountains," which many Hebrew manuscripts, the Septuagint, and the Vulgate read instead as "cities." The reformed John Gill agrees on the substance: these were temples and altars for idols, built on hills and so called high places, and what Jehoram "made" he in truth rebuilt — restoring the very shrines that Asa and Jehoshaphat had thrown down.

On the charge of "fornication" the witnesses are of one mind that the sin is spiritual. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke explains that Israel was joined to Jehovah as a wife to her husband, so that to serve other gods was adultery against him — this is frequently, he says, the only meaning of the terms adultery and fornication in the Scriptures. Ellicott names it the spiritual fornication of unfaithfulness to Jehovah, the only lawful spouse of Israel, in the manner of Hosea's great parable at Hosea 2:5. And the closing word "compelled" both Ellicott and Wesley take at its full weight: Ellicott renders it "seduced," the verb of enticement to idolatry at Deut. 13:6; the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley says the king drew the people not only by his counsel and example but by force, by threats and penalties.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sharpens the tragedy of a king turning his power against the very people he was set to guard. Jehoram caused the men of Jerusalem to commit fornication, seducing them, as it were, to eat things sacrificed to idols in the manner rebuked at Rev. 2:20; the city over which he kept his court he easily drew into his spiritual whoredom, while the country people, harder to corrupt by flattery, he compelled by force. He used, Henry says, the power given him for the edification of the church to work its destruction.

The witnesses do not divide. Ellicott and Gill fix the shrines and their rebuilding; Clarke and Ellicott define the fornication as apostasy; Wesley and Henry expose the compulsion behind it. Between them they show a king who did not merely fall into idolatry himself but dragged a whole people after him, by seduction where he could and by force where he could not — the crime that, in the next verse, will draw down a letter from the greatest of the prophets.
12:
"And there came a writing to him from Elijah the prophet" — the chronicler's one and only mention of the great prophet of the north, and the verse over which the witnesses labour longest, for Elijah seems already to have been taken up to heaven. The reformed John Gill sets the alternatives out and chooses among them: this was not a letter written after Elijah's ascension and sent down years later, as some rabbis fancied, nor the work of some other man of the same name, nor of Elisha bearing his master's name; it was a writing composed by Elijah before his translation, who, foreseeing by the spirit of prophecy what Jehoram would do, wrote it and left it — most likely with Elisha, as Kimchi suggests — to be delivered at the proper time, so that the king might well suppose it came straight from heaven.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry and the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley argue that the difficulty is one of order, not of fact. By this writing, Henry says, it appears that Jehoram came to the throne and showed his true colours before Elijah's translation; for the history of that translation is set out of its proper place, since we read of Jehoshaphat's death and Jehoram's accession, at 1 Kings 22:50, before we read of Elijah being taken up. The prophet's own departure being at hand, so that he could not go in person, he left this writing — probably with Elisha — to be sent when the time came. Wesley reasons in the same way, noting that Elisha's attendance on Jehoshaphat need not mean Elijah was already gone.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke canvasses every theory — an angel from heaven, a prophecy left with Elisha, Elijah put for Elisha, a second Elijah, a letter sent from the prophet's hidden retreat — and, though Kennicott contends that Elisha was the real author, Clarke answers that every Hebrew manuscript and all the ancient versions read "Elijah," and that the chronicler never once names Elisha; he inclines to think the writing a prediction uttered in the prophet's lifetime and only now laid before the king, so that Elijah, though not among mortals, still continued to speak. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott offers both the living prophet and the posthumous document: Elijah, though very old, may still have been alive, his extreme age accounting for a written rather than a personal warning; or, if he was already translated, the writing preserved the substance of his last utterances, put into shape and forwarded by one of his pupils, perhaps Elisha — a reading Ellicott thinks favoured by the indefinite phrase, "a writing," not "a letter."

The message itself all the witnesses hear in the name it invokes — "the LORD God of David thy father" — upbraiding Jehoram with a descent that was now not his honour but the aggravation of his apostasy. Whoever carried it, and however it was framed, the warning was real; and Henry notes the pity of it, that had Jehoram but humbled himself as even Ahab once did at 1 Kings 21:27, he might have found a reprieve — but he threw the writing by as waste-paper, and Elijah seemed to him as one that mocked.
13:
The letter's indictment now reaches its sharpest point — Jehoram has walked in the way of the kings of Israel, made Judah and Jerusalem "go a whoring" like the whoredoms of Ahab's house, and slain his own brethren, who were better than himself. The reformed John Gill glosses the first charge plainly: to walk in the way of the kings of Israel was to worship the calves, and even Baal, with the other idols they served. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott attends to the verb, "to go a whoring," the same word for spiritual fornication used at v.11; "like to the whoredoms" is the infinitive of that verb, as the house of Ahab caused them to commit fornication. It is a term, he notes, that the chronicler had used once before at 1 Chronicles 5:25 and does not employ again — reserved, as it were, for the two blackest apostasies of his book. And the closing accusation, "hast slain thy brethren," he ties back to the fratricide already recorded at v.4.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the verse as the formal charge-sheet of Elijah's letter, laid out under distinct heads: Jehoram's departure from the good ways of God in which he had been bred; his conformity to the ways of the house of Ahab, that impious and scandalous family; his setting up and enforcing idolatry throughout his kingdom; and, blackest of all, his murder of his brethren for no crime but that they were better than himself. The very aggravation that had made him hate them — their piety — is the aggravation the indictment presses: he slew the men whose goodness rebuked his wickedness.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch, reading the letter through to its threatened penalties, treat this verse as the ground on which the sentence of the verses that follow is built: because Jehoram made Judah go a whoring after the manner of Ahab and shed his brothers' blood, the LORD will smite his people, his children, his wives, and his goods, and strike his own body with a wasting disease. The charge and the doom are of one piece.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill names the idols behind "the way of the kings of Israel"; Ellicott fixes the verb of apostasy and its cross-references; Henry marshals the counts of the indictment; Keil binds the crime to the coming punishment. Between them they show that Elijah's writing was no vague reproach but a precise arraignment — every clause naming a specific sin, and every sin about to be answered, measure for measure, in the judgments the letter goes on to pronounce. The brother-slayer who made a nation play the harlot is told, in God's own name, exactly why the blows are about to fall.
14:
"Behold, with a great plague will the LORD smite thy people, and thy children, and thy wives, and all thy goods." The witnesses weigh both the reach of the threatened blow and its justice. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders the Hebrew more starkly — Jehovah is about to smite a great smiting in thy people and in thy sons — and observes that the immediate object of the verb is left unexpressed, for it was Jehoram himself who was to be smitten in his people, his sons, his wives, and all his goods, as v.17 will show. The smiting, he explains, is a heaven-sent stroke, a divine visitation, and it would take the concrete form of an invasion of Philistines and Arabs who sacked Jerusalem and the royal palace. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke adds the Targum's paraphrase, that the Word of the LORD will send a great mortality — reading the plague as a sweeping death among the king's household and realm.

The reformed John Gill fastens on the righteousness of visiting the people for their king's sin: they had gone into the same idolatry with him, and for the most part willingly, and therefore deserved to be smitten — and the smiting of them would itself be a punishment to him, who must watch his kingdom suffer for the apostasy he had led. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry presses the same point into a general truth: bad men bring God's judgments upon all about them. His people justly suffered, Henry says, because they had complied with his idolatry, and his wives because they had drawn him to it; the king's sin becomes a contagion, and those who shared it must share its penalty.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch, reading the letter as a whole, take this verse as the first of the two penalties Elijah announces — the blow upon the king's house and possessions, to be followed by the blow upon his own body in the verse after. The one sentence divides into an outward stroke and an inward, and this is the outward: everything Jehoram had gathered about him — subjects, sons, wives, wealth — marked for a single devastating visitation.

The witnesses do not divide. Ellicott fixes the grammar and names the Philistine invasion that would fulfil it; Clarke supplies the Targum's "mortality"; Gill and Henry justify the falling of the blow on a people who had shared the sin; Keil sets it as the first half of the doom. Between them they show that the threatened plague was no arbitrary cruelty but a measured judgment — the king who had corrupted his whole house and kingdom would be struck precisely there, in the house and kingdom he had corrupted, and would live to see it happen.
15:
"And thou shalt have great sickness by disease of thy bowels, until thy bowels fall out by reason of the sickness day by day." The witnesses read the second and more personal stroke of the sentence, and they hear in it a terrible fitness. The reformed John Gill states it flatly: the disease of the bowels was a just retaliation upon a man who had shown no bowels of compassion toward the brethren he slew. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the same measure-for-measure lesson at length: Asa, whose heart was in the main perfect with God, was diseased only in his feet, but Jehoram, whose heart was wicked, was struck in his very inwards; he that had no bowels of pity for his own flesh and blood was so plagued in his bowels that they fell out of him. And Henry notes the mercy hidden in the warning — the king is told beforehand, that his blood might be upon his own head, the watchman having delivered his soul, and that when the thing came to pass it might be seen to fall not by chance but as the just punishment of his sin.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders the clause literally — "thou thyself shalt be in great diseases through diseasing of thy bowels" — and compares the doubled expression with the language of the covenant curses at Deut. 28:59 and the wounded spirit of Proverbs 18:14. The phrase "day by day," he explains, is literally "days upon days," most probably a year upon a year, or in two years — the very span that v.19 will confirm, in the idiom found also at 1 Samuel 1:3 and Isaiah 29:1.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses fill out the reach of the judgment. Adam Clarke observes that such a falling out of the bowels must have been caused by a violent inflammation, and recalls that by the same dreadful death perished Antiochus Epiphanes and Herod Agrippa — the disease a byword for the end of tyrants. John Wesley, glancing back over the sentence, marks its exact correspondences: the people are smitten because they complied with the king's idolatrous commands, and the wives because their lives should go for the lives of the brethren he had murdered at v.4.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Henry read the disease as retribution upon a pitiless man; Ellicott fixes the Hebrew and the two-year term; Clarke sets Jehoram among the tyrants who died so; Wesley traces the blood-for-blood justice of the whole. Between them they show a punishment fitted to the crime with awful precision — the bowels of the merciless man made the seat of his lingering death, and the very household he had built on murder marked to be carried off in payment for it.
16:
The threatened stroke now takes shape as history: "the LORD stirred up against Jehoram the spirit of the Philistines, and of the Arabians, that were near the Ethiopians." The witnesses trace both the phrase and the peoples. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott explains that to stir up the spirit of a man is to rouse his will to an undertaking, an idiom found at Jeremiah 51:11 and Haggai 1:14, and comparable to the LORD's stirring of the Medes against Babylon at Isaiah 13:17. Philistines and Arabians, he notes, are named together elsewhere as the enemies of Judah, at 2 Chronicles 26:7 and 2 Chronicles 17:11; the invasion accords with the raid denounced at Joel 3:4-6 and is certainly historical. And "near the Ethiopians" he renders "at the hand of," that is beside, the Cushites — some tribes of southern Arabia, for there were Cushite settlements on both sides of the Red Sea.

The reformed John Gill measures the reversal of fortune the invasion marks. These same Philistines had been so cowed in the days of Jehoshaphat that they brought him presents and tribute willingly; now, under his apostate son, they are stirred up to invade. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley presses the same point into a lesson on providence: the Philistines were a people fully subdued and dispirited, but God now raised their spirits and their courage to do his work — the LORD arming against Jehoram the very neighbours his father had tamed. The Arabians called Ethiopians, Wesley adds, were a people of Arabia, so named either for their likeness of complexion to the Africans or because the one people was a colony of the other.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke stands back to weigh the whole calamity. We have, he says, no other account of this war; and though it was but a predatory raid, it proved utterly ruinous and destructive. He sums up the sweep of the divine displeasure in a single exclamation: what a general curse fell upon this bad king — in his body, soul, substance, family, and government! Every sphere of the man's life is struck at once.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch, reading the letter's fulfilment, take this invasion as the outward blow of v.14 now falling — the smiting of the king's people, house, and goods by an enemy God himself has roused. The witnesses do not divide. Ellicott fixes the idiom and the geography of the raiders; Gill marks the reversal from the tribute of Jehoshaphat's day; Wesley reads God arming the dispirited; Clarke names the totality of the curse. Between them they show that the Philistine and Arab bands were no accident of the frontier but the instrument of heaven — the great smiting promised in Elijah's letter, moving now against a king whom God had marked for judgment on every side.
17:
The invasion strikes with a fearful precision — "they came up into Judah, and brake into it, and carried away all the substance that was found in the king's house, and his sons also, and his wives; so that there was never a son left him, save Jehoahaz, the youngest of his sons." The witnesses mark how narrowly the blow was aimed. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders "brake into it" as "clave it asunder," the verb of the divided sea at Exodus 14:16, and infers that the enemy actually entered Jerusalem, though the chronicler, in his desire to be concise, has not expressly said so — just as he omits to state that Shishak captured the city before plundering it at 2 Chronicles 12:9. That the sons were not left means, Ellicott adds, that they were not merely carried off but slain, as 2 Chronicles 22:1 makes plain.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the aim of the raiders as the finger of God. They fought, he observes, neither against small nor great, but against the king's house only; they made straight for it and carried off all its substance, taking captive none but the king's wives and sons — so that God made it evident the controversy was with Jehoram and his house. And Henry hears the law of exact recompense: Jehoram had slain all his brethren to strengthen himself, and now all his sons are slain but one, and so he is weakened. Blood for blood. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley says the very same: the wives too were slain, save Ahaziah and Athaliah who were perhaps hidden away; he had slain all his brethren, and they slay all his sons but one — and that one had not escaped either, Wesley insists, had he not been of the house of David, which must not be extirpated like the house of Ahab, because a blessing was in it, no less than that of the Messiah.

The reformed John Gill notes only that they came up into Judah in hostile array; and the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke settles the identity of the surviving son, who bore, he says, at least three names — Jehoahaz here, Ahaziah at 2 Chronicles 22:1, and Azariah at 2 Chronicles 22:6. Ellicott, more exactly, takes Jehoahaz and Ahaziah for the same name with its elements reversed, meaning "Iah holdeth," and judges the Azariah of the later verse a simple mistake, the versions all reading Ahaziah.

The witnesses do not divide. Ellicott fixes the forcing of the city and the slaughter of the sons; Henry and Wesley read the blood-for-blood justice and the covenant reason one son was spared; Gill and Clarke settle the fact and the survivor's name. Between them they show the judgment falling exactly where the sin had been — the fratricide answered in the slaughter of a house, and a single heir left alive not for the father's sake but for the promise's, that the lamp of David might not go out.
18:
"And after all this the LORD smote him in his bowels with an incurable disease." Having lost his house, the king is struck in his own body, and the witnesses read this as the second and inward stroke of the sentence. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch mark the turn precisely: the first punishment had fallen upon Jehoram's people, sons, wives, and goods; now the second falls upon his own flesh. The reformed John Gill canvasses what the disease may have been — some have thought a rupture, some the falling of the fundament or a fistula, some the colic or iliac passion, but the general opinion, he says, is that it was a dysentery, a bloody flux; and he records the Targum's grim phrase, that the Word of the LORD broke him.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott secures the force of "incurable," which is literally "to a disease, to want of healing" — a sickness past all remedy, the same expression of hopeless hurt used at 2 Chronicles 36:16 of a people beyond cure. He notes too that the Syriac and Arabic versions draw vv.16-18 together as all part of Elijah's prophecy, so that the invasion and the disease alike stand as the fulfilment of the letter's threat.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry pictures the affliction in its full misery. The disease was very grievous, he says, seated in the bowels and producing a continual griping, and with it there was a complication of other sore diseases; and it was as tedious as it was grievous, for it held him two full years and could get no relief, being incurable though the king was in the prime of life, not yet forty years old. Here, Henry reflects, was a man struck where he had been most pitiless — and yet he is careful to add that even good men, dear to God, may be visited with such diseases, only to them they are fatherly chastisements, borne up by divine consolation, whereas to Jehoram they were the unmixed stroke of judgment.

The witnesses do not divide. Keil marks the shift from the outward blow to the inward; Gill weighs the physicians' guesses and settles on the bloody flux; Ellicott fixes the word "incurable" and the versions that bind the whole judgment into one prophecy; Henry unfolds the length and anguish of it. Between them they show the promise of v.15 beginning to work itself out in the king's body — a slow, humiliating, hopeless sickness settling into the very seat of the compassion he had never shown, and running its appointed two years to the wretched end the next verse records.
19:
"And it came to pass, that in process of time, after the end of two years, his bowels fell out by reason of his sickness; so he died of sore diseases. And his people made no burning for him, like the burning of his fathers." The witnesses attend to the exact fulfilment of the time and the dishonour of the end. The reformed John Gill notes simply that for two years the king was tortured with the disease before it killed him. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott presses the wording: "in process of time" is literally "at days upon days," and the following clause, "about the time of the going forth of the end of two years," fixes the moment when two full years after the delivery of Elijah's prediction had expired — the time of the event, he remarks, exactly coinciding with the time foretold. The disease he takes for a violent dysentery, and the phrase "by reason of his sickness" as "along with," that is during, his disease.

His fellow grammatical-historical witness Keil and Delitzsch labours over the same difficult Hebrew, rejecting the easy reading that treats the words as a mere periphrasis for "the end of two years," and rendering rather that when a number of days had passed, at the time of the expiration of the term, his bowels came out during the sickness, and the king died in sore pains. Both witnesses agree on the outcome and on the shame that followed: his people made no burning for him.

That withheld honour the witnesses read as the studied verdict of a nation. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke explains that his people made no burning of aromatic woods for him as they had for his forefathers, pointing back to the honours paid at 2 Chronicles 16:14; and he cites the Targum's picture of a constipation and inflammation of the bowels ending in their gushing out. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the sting of the omission: the king's memory was so far from sweet and precious to his people that they would not honour it with any spices or sweet odours, though his body, after so long and loathsome a disease, surely needed something to perfume it. Even a people prone to idolatry, Henry observes, had no real kindness for their idolatrous king.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the two years' torment; Ellicott and Keil wrestle the Hebrew and mark how the death fell exactly at the predicted term; Clarke and Henry read the unhonoured funeral as the nation's own judgment on the man. Between them they show Elijah's letter vindicated to the hour — the bowels fallen out, the king dead in agony at the appointed time, and a people so weary of him that they denied his corpse the customary fire, the very dishonour that Jeremiah would one day pronounce over another godless king of the line at Jeremiah 22:18-19.
20:
The reign closes on a note of unrelieved contempt — "thirty and two years old was he when he began to reign, and he reigned in Jerusalem eight years, and departed without being desired. Howbeit they buried him in the city of David, but not in the sepulchres of the kings." The witnesses linger over the strange, cold epitaph. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch explain the repetition of the king's age and the length of his reign, already given at v.5, by the fact that this closing section is drawn from a special source in which those notes stood again — a supposition supported by the peculiar language and the absence of the historian's usual formulae. The phrase "without being desired" they render "mourned by none," from a word meaning desire or longing, so that the king died desired of no one; and they correct Luther, who followed the Vulgate in taking it to mean he walked in a way that was not right — the word speaks not of his walk but of the void his death left, which was none. Buried in the city of David he was, yet not in the graves of the kings, and by that exclusion, Keil says, a judgment was pronounced upon him.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott agrees at every point. He notes that the word "years" has actually dropped out of the Hebrew text here, though some manuscripts keep it, and that the repetition of the regnal figures marks the writer transcribing from another authority. "Departed without being desired" he glosses "died unregretted," the Hebrew answering the Latin desiderium; and the burial "not in the sepulchres of the kings," a further circumstance of dishonour not recorded in 2 Kings 8:17, he sets beside the like disgrace of other bad kings at 2 Chronicles 24:25 and 2 Chronicles 26:23, and compares Jeremiah's word over Jehoiakim, that they shall not lament for him, at Jeremiah 22:18-19. He records, only to reject it, the charge of the critic Thenius that these additions to Jehoram's history betray not merely tradition but pure embellishment on the chronicler's part; the grounds Thenius alleges, Ellicott answers, are themselves misinterpretations of the statements of Kings.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke and the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry drive home the moral of the loveless funeral. The king, Clarke says, was hated while he lived and neglected when he died, visibly cursed of God and execrated by the people he had lived only to corrupt and oppress; no annalist troubled to write his life, and this summary notice consigns him to the execration of posterity, holding up to every ruler the rock on which he wrecked the state. Henry adds that nobody valued him living or lamented him dead; they would not bury him among the kings, thinking him unworthy to lie with them, and the exclusion of his body from his fathers' sepulchres may serve, Henry suggests, as an intimation of the everlasting separation of the wicked from the spirits of just men — for those that despise God shall be lightly esteemed.

The witnesses do not divide. Keil and Ellicott fix the text, the special source, and the true sense of "undesired"; Clarke and Henry read the unhonoured grave as the final verdict of God and man alike. Between them they close the reign as it deserved — a king who forsook the God of his fathers laid, at the last, apart from his fathers, mourned by no one and remembered only as a warning.
6:
"He walked in the way of the kings of Israel, like as did the house of Ahab; for he had the daughter of Ahab to wife." The witnesses fasten on that marriage as the hinge of the whole apostasy. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott notes that the sentence is a repetition, word for word, of the indictment at 2 Kings 8:18 — the chronicler is content to take over the older verdict unchanged. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke names the wife: this was Athaliah, daughter of Ahab and Jezebel, as famous for her impieties and cruelty as her most profligate mother, and it is likely, Clarke judges, that she was the principal cause of Jehoram's own cruelty and profaneness. The marriage into Ahab's house is thus, for the witnesses, no incidental detail but the very conduit by which the idolatry and bloodshed of Samaria flowed into Jerusalem.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the verse as the head of the section running through the revolts of Edom and Libnah: because Joram walked in the way of the kings of Israel and did evil in the eyes of the LORD, the LORD would not for all that destroy his house — the mercy of the next verse standing in deliberate contrast to the sin of this one. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the practical shape of that evil: Jehoram walked in the way of the house of Ahab, made the high places which the people were always too forward to build, and did his utmost to set up idolatry again, ruining the reformation his good father and grandfather had so carefully carried on.

Henry draws the lesson that a man's affinities are his undoing: the son of godly Jehoshaphat, married to the daughter of ungodly Ahab, took the character of the house he married into rather than the house he was born into. The reforming line of Asa and Jehoshaphat is reversed in a single reign, and reversed through a wife. The witnesses do not divide. Ellicott secures the borrowed wording; Clarke fixes the guilty marriage and its baleful influence; Keil sets the sin against the mercy that follows; Henry unfolds the wreckage of the reformation. Between them they show that Jehoram's evil was not a private vice but a policy of the throne, imported with Athaliah and imposed upon the kingdom — the calf-worship and Baal-worship of the north now planted in the city of David, so that the difference between the two kingdoms, which Jehoshaphat had laboured to preserve, was all but effaced. It is against this dark backdrop that the covenant faithfulness of God, in the verse that follows, shines the more astonishingly.
7:
Against the sin just named the chronicler sets the mercy that outlasts it — "the LORD would not destroy the house of David, because of the covenant that he had made with David." The witnesses find here the deepest note of the reign. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch observe that the chronicler has recast the thought of the parallel: where 2 Kings 8:19 reads that the LORD would not destroy Judah for David his servant's sake, the chronicler writes that he would not destroy the house of David because of the covenant that he had made with David, and would give him a lamp, and his sons, for ever — a small insertion, they note, that brings the promise to the sons more prominently forward.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott defends this as an exegetical, not an arbitrary, expansion of the older text, against the critic who called it a mere deviation. He weighs the phrase "the covenant that he made for David," comparing the like construction at Isaiah 55:3, "I will make an everlasting covenant for you, even the sure mercies of David" — a form of words, he observes, generally used of the stronger imposing terms on the weaker, as at Joshua 9:6 and 1 Samuel 11:1-2. The promised "light" he renders literally "a lamp," and notes that many Hebrew manuscripts, with the Septuagint, Vulgate, and Targum, read "and to his sons" just as here. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke glosses the lamp with a single stroke: to give a light to David is "to give him a descendant," an unbroken line upon his throne.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws out the theology the covenant contains. God was tender of his covenant with the house of David, Henry says, and therefore would not destroy the royal family, wretchedly corrupted and degenerate as it now was. The tenour of that covenant was exactly this — that David's seed should be visited with the rod for their transgressions, yet the covenant itself should never be broken, as the great charter of Ps. 89:30 and following declares. And Henry names the reason the line could not be extinguished: there was a blessing in it, no less a blessing than that of the Messiah, so that when the houses of Jeroboam, Baasha, and Ahab were destroyed root and branch, David's house, though sometimes brought as low as this, must be preserved.

The witnesses do not divide. Keil and Ellicott secure the wording and its covenant grammar; Clarke reads the lamp as the promised heir; Henry unfolds the covenant that keeps the flame alight. Between them they show why a king so evil could not simply be swept away: the throne he disgraced was pledged to a coming Son, and the God he forsook would not forsake his own oath.
8:
"In his days the Edomites revolted from under the dominion of Judah, and made themselves a king." The witnesses read the loss of Edom as the first outward sign that heaven had turned against the throne. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sets the revolt in its history: it answers the notice at 2 Kings 8:20, and he recalls from 1 Kings 22:47 that under Jehoshaphat there had been no king in Edom but only a deputy, a viceroy who governed the province for Judah. Under the father Edom was a subject vassal; under the son it broke free and set up a king of its own — a plain reversal of the strength the kingdom had enjoyed in its faithful days. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke passes the reader to the fuller account of the same revolt at 2 Kings 8:21.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch, treating this and the following verses together, read the whole notice of Edom's and Libnah's revolt as gathered up by the chronicler under a single explanation, which he will state outright at v.10 — that these rebellions befell because he had forsaken the LORD God of his fathers. The political fact and the spiritual cause are bound together: the king who abandoned the God of his fathers found the dominion of his fathers slipping from his hand.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry presses exactly that connection into a general rule. When Jehoram forsook God and his worship, Henry observes, his subjects withdrew from their allegiance to him: some of the tributary provinces abroad did so, and the Edomites revolted, and though he chastised them, as the next verse will tell, he could not reduce them again. There is a righteousness in it, Henry hears — the ruler who casts off his allegiance to the King of kings can hardly wonder when his own subjects cast off their allegiance to him.

The witnesses do not divide. Ellicott and Clarke fix the fact against the parallel and recover the earlier state of Edom under a Judean deputy; Keil binds the revolt to its stated moral cause; Henry draws the abiding lesson. Between them they show that the empire Jehoshaphat had held was already coming apart in his son's hands — not by the chance of politics but by the withdrawal of the divine favour that had held it together. Edom's new king is the first crack in a dominion that apostasy is quietly dissolving, and the sword Jehoram will raise to recover it, in the verse that follows, will not avail against a judgment already gone forth.
9:
"Then Jehoram went forth with his princes, and all his chariots with him; and he rose up by night, and smote the Edomites which compassed him in, and the captains of the chariots." The witnesses read this not, as a hasty eye might, as a victory, but as a narrow escape. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders the opening "and Jehoram passed over," and takes "his princes" to mean his captains; where the parallel at 2 Kings 8:21 reads that he went over "to Zair," Ellicott judges "Zair" a corruption of "Seir," the mountain-land of Edom, so that the chronicler has quietly substituted an intelligible phrase for an obscure one. But the heart of his reading is the character of the action. Brief as the notice is, Ellicott insists it relates no triumph of Jehoram's but his desperate plight: rising by night, he had to cut his way out through the enemy's troops which had surrounded him and his forces — the smiting is the smiting of a trapped man hacking through the ring that hemmed him in.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch confirm the point from the words that close the parallel account: at the end of 2 Kings 8:21 it is added that "the people fled to their tents" — the notice, that is, of the collapse of Joram's attempt to bring Edom again under his dominion. The king broke out with his life and his chariotry, but the campaign failed; Edom was not recovered. Keil weighs too the small textual divergence between the chronicler's "with his captains" and the disputed word of Kings, the kind of variation that so often separates the two records.

So the witnesses turn what looks like a feat of arms into a confession of defeat. The chariots and the night attack are real, but they are the marks of a king surrounded and struggling to survive, not of a conqueror imposing his will. Ellicott recovers the true shape of the event and mends the corrupted place-name; Keil supplies from Kings the sentence that seals its failure. Between them they let the verse serve the chapter's argument: the sword Jehoram raised against the revolt of v.8 availed him nothing, for the judgment behind the revolt could not be beaten back by any midnight sally. He escaped the encircling Edomites only to leave Edom lost — a fitting emblem of a reign that spent its strength and gained nothing, because the God of its fathers had been forsaken.
10:
"So the Edomites revolted from under the hand of Judah unto this day. The same time also did Libnah revolt from under his hand, because he had forsaken the LORD God of his fathers." The witnesses gather around the second revolt and the reason the chronicler gives for both. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott notes that the phrase "unto this day," as at 2 Chronicles 5:9, fixes a date some time before the captivity, and that no account is here taken of Amaziah's later and probably impermanent reduction of Edom at 2 Chronicles 25:11-15. He marks the exact seam of the sources: the parallel at 2 Kings 8:22 ends with the bare mention of Libnah, and it is the chronicler who adds both "from under his hand" and, crucially, the moral ground of the rebellion — for he had forsaken Jehovah, the God of his fathers.

Ellicott then presses what that forsaking meant, and clears away two lesser explanations. He will not follow the critic Thenius, who supposed that Libnah, as a city of the priests, refused obedience to an idolatrous king, nor Hitzig, who read the revolt as a merely religious secession. Jehoram forsook Jehovah, rather, by walking in the way of the kings of Israel as did the house of Ahab — that is, by adopting and popularising the worship of the Tyrian Baal to please his wife and her people; for in those days, Ellicott observes, friendship with an alien race seems to have involved the recognition of their gods, as the alliance of Tyre and Judah at Amos 1:9 may imply.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley and the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry read the revolt with one voice. Libnah, Wesley says, set up for a free state; and the reason is here given both why God permitted it and why they did it — because Jehoram had become an idolater: while he adhered to God, they adhered to him; but when he cast God off, they cast him off. Henry adds that Libnah had of old been a royal city with a king of its own, at Joshua 12:15, and that its people shook off Jehoram's government because they could not remain subject to an idolater without danger of being drawn from God themselves; and whether or not that justified their revolt, Henry says, it certainly justifies the providence of God which ordered it so.

So the witnesses converge on the chronicler's own verdict, and the debate is only over the lesser readings Ellicott sets aside. Edom lost for good, Libnah broken away, the empire crumbling at its edges — and behind every crack the one cause the sacred writer will not let the reader miss: a king who forsook the God of his fathers, and a kingdom that began, province by province, to forsake him.
